articles.title: He taught film dance for a living, then taught himself keyboard, guitar and drums
articles.deck: Ricky Biswasi led an orchestra in Jeypore singing film songs. He talks about the year his friends left, the verse that stopped him, and why he no longer thinks of prayer as asking.

hero.alt: Ricky Biswasi playing a Korg keyboard during a service, with the congregation and a lit cross behind him

interviewMeta.subject: Ricky Biswasi
interviewMeta.subjectBio: A worship leader in Jeypore, Odisha, who leads the Elohim Worship Team and teaches keyboard, guitar and drums to young people in his church. Entirely self-taught.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the January 2013 issue. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is otherwise unchanged.

body.v: Ricky Biswasi is a young aspiring worship leader who has a great heart for worship and the church. One of the things that impresses us most about him is that he is self-taught musically.

But this did not happen all of a sudden. He was a very active guy, using his skills for the enjoyment of worldly desires. He has been famous in his society for his choreography talent. As he was living a lifestyle without vision, he found himself failed in the sight of God.

It was not too late that he left everything that dishonest God, and now uses all the talents and gifts for the glory of the Kingdom. Please read his story to encourage yourself, how you can also be a part of His kingdom with your gifts.
“I never accepted Him until a certain time”
5Talents: Hello Ricky, greetings from 5Talents. How are you?
I am doing well by the grace of God. Thank you!
5Talents: When and how did you come in faith in Christ Jesus as your personal saviour?

I have been born and brought up in a Christian family. Even though I know about Jesus Christ since my childhood, I never accepted Him as my personal saviour and Lord until a certain time. As I have been growing older, I have developed debating, feeling covetous, unfriendly to each and every person in the community I lived.

As Samson's weakness was anger, but still God used his negative actions into positive fashion — God has moulded my life too in a similar style, by speaking to me through His word and prayer. As I kept on meditating upon His word, the Holy Spirit talked to me and taught me to build a positive attitude for others. One day, I accepted Jesus Christ as my personal saviour and my Lord, and since then I have been following Christ.
“I started to play without any knowledge of chords”
5Talents: Please share about the talents you have received from God.

I believe talents are a gift from God. I have been a dancer from my childhood and I used to teach young boys and girls to dance for film songs. Subsequently, knowing the truth and accepting Jesus as my saviour, I left teaching dance for film, and rather I started to teach dance for youth in church and also started a worship team.

There was a keyboard in my church which has attracted me towards it. I started to play without any knowledge of chords and combinations. Miraculously, God helped me to understand in stages, and whereas my father has also been teaching me basic concepts in keyboard. By practising regularly, I learned playing keyboard and then I started learning guitar too. Even I could gain knowledge regarding playing guitar by the grace of God. I used to wonder how God has gifted me with such talents — and yes, it is only by His grace.

As days passed, I learned playing drums too, and God has enabled me to lead the Sunday worship service, the youth worship service, and also to preach His word and to testify what He has done in my life amongst youth. Indeed, God has given me the privilege to set an example before youth and teach them how to play keyboard, guitar and drums.
“I just resolved to leave everything”
5Talents: When did you know you wanted to be a worship leader?

In 1999, I have been in an orchestra team where I was the team leader, singing secular songs and performing stage programs. Afterwards, I felt tired of all these things and came to know that I shouldn't be using my talent in such a way which I have been using till now.
Even everyone that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him.
body.highlight: I have created him for my glory

body.v: God talked to me with the verse from Isaiah 43:7. When I read this verse I just resolved to leave everything and live my whole life for what I'm made for.

And it's 1999 when I watched some Hillsong worship videos. Touched by it, I always wanted to do such a team in our church. Since then I started learning music and in the word of God, so that one day this type of team will be established and be a wonderful cause to make people glorify God.

Then I got an opportunity to go to Hyderabad, and there I led worship and learned new songs in a church. After one year I came back and continued with my team, the Elohim Worship Team. In this way the church anointed me as a worship leader.
“Worship is a lifestyle”
5Talents: What does a lifestyle of worship mean to you?

Worship is a lifestyle. First of all, worship means just not singing, dancing, modern looks etc, but presenting our bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God. It's the lifestyle of a worshipper. God has forgiven us so that we can forgive others. We should worship God in spirit, truth, with all our mind, soul and strength.

As a worshipper, when we talk, everyone should feel the presence of God, and when people see our face then they should see Jesus, not us. As John the Baptist said in John 3:30, “I must be decreased and He must be increased.” Likewise we should be decreased and hide ourselves in Him and say like Paul, “…not I but Christ.” It's the lifestyle of a worshipper — not I but Christ. And second thing, “Love your neighbour”: we should be an example to the world by helping those in need as Christ did.
“I never felt that I should ask anything”
5Talents: How would you define your prayer life?

God is always faithful in everything and in every situation. He provides me abundantly before I ask or think, so I never felt that I should ask anything. Prayer means asking something. I close my eyes and praise and give thanks to God every time, and I take this habit as prayer.

I talk with God always. My friends left me in the year of 2002 and I became alone, and I started the habit of prayer from that year. Every day I sit before my best friend to tell everything to Him, and that is my prayer life. My best friend Jesus gives me everything whatever I think, even before asking in prayer. So I have only one job now — to praise and give thanks to Him.
“That was my first composition”
5Talents: How has Christ inspired you in composing music?

When I was in class 8th I wrote a song in a sad frame of mind, but not about God — that was about myself. All the words were there about my feelings and my thoughts about my life, and that was my first composition.

But after my matriculation, when I started to meditate on God's word, I found myself that what I am thinking about my life is totally different in the sight of God our Abba Father. When I knew that there is nothing that I should boast for, only one thing is there to boast, and that is I know Jesus Christ our saviour and the true God who gave His blood and bore everything for me. And one thing inspired me a lot, that He came so that I may have life ABUNDANTLY (John 10:10). Hallelujah!

I always listened to the words of the thief (Satan), but when I started listening to my saviour, redeemer, shelter, my greatest love, I forgot everything of my life and started writing about Him alone.
Being discouraged
5Talents: Being a teen leader, have you experienced others discouraging you? If yes, how do you manage the situation?

Yes, many times my heart and my soul fail to manage some critical situations, as I am a youth leader, but God gives me strength in my heart and soul to manage in a unique way in such situations. As it is written in the Bible (Matthew 18:15–20): “If your brother or sister sins, go and point out their fault, just between the two of you. If they listen to you, you have won them over. But if they will not listen, take one or two others along, so that every matter may be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.” So I follow this rule of the Bible.

I was a big sinner and had done many things from which people could find some remarkable things to gossip and to backbite about me. Whenever I am facing such type of dispiriting situations, then I remember one thing: that Lord Jesus came for the sinners, not for the righteous people. Though I'm a sinner from my birth, I trust in God and His mighty power makes me clean every day. Only through the blood, through the word, through the Church, I'm a winner in Christ — and so whoever trusts in Jesus overcomes this world.
5Talents: What would you say to the one who is talented but is sad because they are not given an opportunity to use it, or the talent is not recognized by others?

Everything has its own time according to God's will, and talents should be used to glorify God in any ways. I mean to say that a worshipper should worship, adore and praise Him at all times. It's not important where he or she is — wherever he or she is taking breath, he or she should worship. And it is written in Psalms 37:4 that “Be glad in God and He will give you the desires of your heart.” So we should begin to be glad in God, and He will give us opportunities in a proper manner, and according to His will our talents will be shining to all.

articles.title: Two things you can say when you wake up, and they decide the rest of the day
articles.deck: “Good Lord, it's morning” or “Good morning, Lord.” Lorita Das on gratitude, on the exercise of imagining you have lost everything, and on why humility is not the same as being a doormat.

archiveMeta.editNote: Published as it appeared in the January 2013 issue. Column reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; the wording is otherwise unchanged.

body.v: “If the only prayer you said was ‘thank you’, that would be enough.” — Meister Eckhart

When we wake up in the morning, we have one of two possible expressions that govern our day. Either it is the overwhelming gasp of tension, “Good Lord! It's morning!” or the exuberant shout of joy, “Good morning, Lord!”

If we happen to fall in the first category (which, I am pretty sure, most of us do), we push ourselves through the day complaining about the world's problems and behaving as if all the burdens have fallen on our shoulders. But if we happen to fall in the second category, we start the day on a grateful note and sail through it in a calm and relaxed manner — rejoicing, marvelling and appreciating the Lord's gifts.
An attitude of gratitude

As Christians, we should always carry an attitude of gratitude — counting your blessings, noticing simple pleasures and acknowledging everything that you receive. Most often we focus on what we lack instead of what we have, taking for granted the good things already present in our lives. We complain about not having a house big enough, or enough clothes, or a bigger paycheck. And we wish we could do things differently.

For such people, we have a ‘gratitude exercise’. Imagine losing some of the things that you take for granted — such as your family, your friends, your ability to see or hear, or anything that currently gives you comfort. Then imagine getting each of these things back, one by one, and consider how grateful you would be for each and every one.
Humility
There is another virtue which goes hand in hand with gratitude. Proverbs 27:2 says, “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; someone else and not your own lips.”

God detests pride because it is a sin where we put ourselves in God's place. In this era of ‘marketing’, we cannot resist the urge to self-promote and blow our own trumpets. We idolise ourselves and become self-important and egotistic.

The only way to eliminate ego is humility — an attitude of personal modesty. Humble people are not spineless or doormats, as otherwise thought. Instead they are people with their feet firmly planted on the ground, and rightfully placing God before themselves. Sometimes our achievements and our accomplishments make us blind to the fact that it is indeed the Lord who has made us who we are and given us what we have.
The fullest and best ears of corn hang lowest toward the ground.
body.attr: Bishop Reynolds, quoted by the author

body.v: But all is not over. Take a moment each day and make a list of 5 things to thank God for. Let it not be just a formality; acknowledge His gifts and thank Him wholeheartedly for the blessings and joys that He continues to shower upon you each day.

articles.title: A shoemaker who taught himself six languages, and spent seven years in India without a single convert
articles.deck: William Carey was apprenticed indoors because sunlight blistered his skin. He made a globe out of scrap leather, and did not stop for forty-one years. “I can plod,” he said, when asked to account for himself.

archiveMeta.editNote: The 2012 version of this piece was not original work and has been replaced. This is a new article, written from the nineteenth-century biographies and Carey's own Enquiry, listed at the foot.

body.v: This piece first ran in our January 2013 issue. That version was not our own writing and has been replaced. What follows is new work, researched from Carey's own writing and from the nineteenth-century biographies. Sources are listed at the end.
He was put to shoemaking because he could not work outside. Sunlight blistered his skin, so a boy from a weaver's family in Northamptonshire was apprenticed to an indoor trade and sat at a bench.

He kept a book open on that bench. By twenty-one he had taught himself Latin, Greek, Hebrew and Italian, and was starting on Dutch and French. He made a globe of the world out of scraps of leather, and marked on it what he could find out about every country: the size, the population, what people believed there.
Somebody called that cottage Carey's College. It was a cobbler's front room.
Paulerspury
William Carey was born on 17 August 1761 in a thatched cottage in Paulerspury, an ordinary Northamptonshire village. His family were weavers and he was not sent to be educated.

At around eighteen he left the Church of England, joined the Congregational church at Hackleton where he was apprenticed, and married there in 1781. He began walking the five miles to Olney and back looking for people who would argue theology with him. Olney was a stronghold of the Particular Baptists, and he was baptised among them in October 1783. Two years later he moved to Moulton to be a schoolmaster, and a year after that became the pastor of its small Baptist congregation.
He was, at this point, a village pastor with no money, no standing and no formal education, who could read six languages.
A book about a sea voyage
What set him off was not a sermon. It was a travel book.
My attention to missions was first awakened after I was at Moulton, by reading the Last Voyage of Captain Cook.
body.highlight: by reading the Last Voyage of Captain Cook

body.v: Most readers took Cook's journals as adventure. Carey read them as a population census. He started reading everything he could find that bore on the subject, making notes, filling in the leather globe.

When he raised the question at a ministers' meeting — whether the command to teach all nations still bound ministers now — an older man told him to sit down, and that when God chose to reach the nations He would do it without Carey's help. He did not sit down. In 1792 he published An Enquiry Into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens, which surveyed the history of missions, then went country by country through the known world with the size, the population and the religion of each, and then dealt with the practical question of how any of it could actually be done.
It is an odd document to read now. Half sermon, half spreadsheet. The spreadsheet half is why it worked.

That May he preached at Nottingham on what became the sentence he is remembered for: expect great things from God, attempt great things for God. The Baptist Missionary Society was founded at Kettering that October. Carey had no money to put into the subscription and pledged the profits from his book instead.
Serampore
He sailed in 1793. His wife Dorothy did not want to go, and after two returns from the docks to persuade her, she and the children came.

The East India Company would not have missionaries in its territory, so the work ended up at Serampore, a small Danish colony on the Hooghly north of Calcutta, where the Danish governor would have them and the Company could not reach them. The whole enterprise ran for years out of a foreign enclave fifteen miles from British power.

What they built there was a printing house. Carey learned the languages, ran the presses, and by the time he died the Scriptures had been translated and printed in around forty languages and dialects — Bengali, Sanskrit, Marathi, Assamese, Oriya and on down the list. He wrote grammars and dictionaries for languages that had never had one. He printed the first prose books in Bengali, and helped start the first Bengali newspaper. He taught at Fort William College, and in 1818 he and his colleagues founded Serampore College, which was chartered by Denmark to grant degrees and admitted students regardless of caste or religion. It is still open.

He was also, seriously and not as a hobby, a botanist. He kept a five-acre garden at Serampore, corresponded with Kew, published on Indian flora and in 1820 founded the Agri-Horticultural Society of India, arguing that better agriculture was a straightforwardly good thing to give a country. A genus of flowering plant is named after him.

And he campaigned for years against sati, the burning of widows on their husbands' funeral pyres. He collected the evidence and kept putting it in front of the administration. When the practice was finally prohibited in 1829, the edict was handed to him on a Sunday morning to be translated into Bengali. He gave up preaching that day and translated it immediately, so that it could take effect without losing a week.
What it cost
Seven years passed in India before a single Indian person came to faith through their work. Seven years is a very long time to be wrong in public.

In March 1812 the Serampore printing house burned down. It took the presses, the type for a dozen languages, the paper, and the manuscripts — years of translation, including a polyglot dictionary he had been compiling. Work that could not be reconstructed from anything. He began again.

The hardest part of the account is his family. A five-year-old son, Peter, died of dysentery early on. Dorothy — who had not wanted to come, who lost a child in a country she had no wish to be in — became severely mentally ill and remained so for about twelve years until her death in 1807. She is a real cost of this story and she did not choose it. Any honest telling of Carey has to sit with that rather than move past it, and most tellings do move past it.
Why he is still known

He is called the father of modern missions, which is a title that flattens him. What he actually was is a translator, a printer, a lexicographer, a botanist and a college founder, who worked in one place for forty-one years and never once went home on leave.
He died at Serampore on 9 June 1834, aged seventy-two. He had asked that a friend not talk about Dr Carey after he was gone, but about Dr Carey's God.
So what, in 2026?
Somebody once asked what accounted for what he had done. His answer was two words: “I can plod.”

That is a strange thing to read now. Everything around you is built to suggest that the way things happen is fast — that you find the thing, it takes off, and if it does not take off in a reasonable time you were wrong about it. Seven years of no result is not a season anyone plans for.

Carey had seven of them, then a fire that took the work back to nothing, and then he did it again. He was not unusually gifted at any single thing except staying. If you are trying to work out whether to keep going with something slow, he is not an inspiring story so much as a plain piece of evidence: the compounding is real, and almost nobody is around long enough to collect it.

Sources: William Carey, An Enquiry Into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792); Eustace Carey, Memoir of William Carey (1836); George Smith, The Life of William Carey, Shoemaker and Missionary (1885), at the Christian Classics Ethereal Library; S. Pearce Carey, William Carey (1923); and the records of Serampore College and of the Agri-Horticultural Society of India.
